claim: The mushroom body (MB) is the major site of associative learning in Drosophila.
source: In Drosophila, the mushroom body (MB) is the major site of associative learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research establishing the MB's role in learning.

claim: The adult MB's α lobe contains 983 neurons within three functional compartments.
source: We reconstructed the morphologies and synaptic connections of all 983 neurons within the three functional units, or compartments, that compose the adult MB's α lobe, using a dataset of isotropic 8 nm voxels collected by focused ion-beam milling scanning electron microscopy.
evidence: This claim is based on the direct counting and reconstruction of neurons in the EM dataset.

claim: Kenyon cells (KCs) make multiple en passant synapses to MB output neurons (MBONs) in each compartment.
source: We found that Kenyon cells (KCs), whose sparse activity encodes sensory information, each make multiple en passant synapses to MB output neurons (MBONs) in each compartment.
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of synaptic connections in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Some MBONs have inputs from all KCs, while others differentially sample sensory modalities.
source: Some MBONs have inputs from all KCs, while others differentially sample sensory modalities.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of connectivity patterns in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Only 6% of KC>MBON synapses receive a direct synapse from a dopaminergic neuron (DAN).
source: Only 6% of KC>MBON synapses receive a direct synapse from a dopaminergic neuron (DAN).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of synaptic connections in the EM reconstruction.

claim: KC>DAN synapses exist in the mushroom body α lobe.
source: We identified two unanticipated classes of synapses, KC>DAN and DAN>MBON.
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of synaptic connections in the EM reconstruction.

claim: DAN>MBON synapses exist in the mushroom body α lobe.
source: We identified two unanticipated classes of synapses, KC>DAN and DAN>MBON.
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of synaptic connections in the EM reconstruction.

claim: DAN activation produces a slow depolarization of the MBON in DAN>MBON synapses.
source: DAN activation produces a slow depolarization of the MBON in these DAN>MBON synapses and can weaken memory recall.
evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiological recordings showing MBON responses to DAN stimulation.

claim: DAN activation can weaken memory recall.
source: DAN activation produces a slow depolarization of the MBON in these DAN>MBON synapses and can weaken memory recall.
evidence: This claim is based on behavioral experiments showing reduced conditioned responses when DANs are activated during memory testing.

claim: The mushroom body (MB) is the center of associative learning in insects.
source: The mushroom body (MB) is the center of associative learning in insects (Erber et al., 1980; Heisenberg et al., 1985; de Belle and Heisenberg, 1994; Dubnau et al., 2001; McGuire et al., 2001; Mizunami et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Sensory information enters the MB via the calyx, where the dendritic claws of Kenyon cells (KCs) receive synaptic inputs from projection neurons of olfactory and other modalities including visual, gustatory and thermal.
source: Sensory information enters the MB via the calyx, where the dendritic claws of Kenyon cells (KCs) receive synaptic inputs from projection neurons of olfactory and other modalities including visual, gustatory and thermal (Vogt et al., 2016; Kirkhart and Scott, 2015; Yagi et al., 2016; Caron et al., 2013; Stocker et al., 1990; Wong et al., 2002; Strausfeld, 1976; Tanaka et al., 2004; Liu et al., 2015; Frank et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The parallel axonal fibers of the KCs form the MB-lobes, the output region of the MB.
source: The parallel axonal fibers of the KCs form the MB-lobes, the output region of the MB.
evidence: This claim is based on established anatomical knowledge of the MB structure.

claim: A pattern of sparse activity in the KC population represents the identity of the stimulus.
source: A pattern of sparse activity in the KC population represents the identity of the stimulus.
evidence: This claim is based on prior physiological studies of KC activity patterns.

claim: Sparseness in KC activity is maintained through two mechanisms: individual KCs generally only spike when they receive simultaneous inputs from multiple projection neurons, and overall KC excitability is regulated by feedback inhibition from a GABAergic neuron, MB-APL.
source: This sparseness is maintained through two mechanisms. First, individual KCs generally only spike when they receive simultaneous inputs from multiple projection neurons (Gruntman and Turner, 2013). Second, overall KC excitability is regulated by feedback inhibition from a GABAergic neuron, MB-APL, that arborizes throughout the MB (Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014a; Tanaka et al., 2008; Liu and Davis, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research on KC physiology and APL function.

claim: Only a small subset of KCs respond to a given sensory stimulus.
source: Thus, only a small subset of KCs respond to a given sensory stimulus (Perez-Orive et al., 2002; Turner et al., 2008; Honegger et al., 2011; Murthy et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior physiological studies.

claim: Dopaminergic or octopaminergic neurons convey information of punishment or reward and induce memories that associate the sensory stimulus with its valence.
source: Upon this representation of the sensory world, dopaminergic or octopaminergic neurons convey information of punishment or reward and induce memories that associate the sensory stimulus with its valence (Schroll et al., 2006; Schwaerzel et al., 2003; Liu et al., 2012; Burke et al., 2012; Riemensperger et al., 2005; Mao and Davis, 2009; Heisenberg, 2003; Claridge-Chang et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on reinforcement signaling in the MB.

claim: The parallel axonal fibers of ~2000 KCs in each MB can be divided into 16 compartmental units by the dendrites of 21 types of MB output neurons (MBONs) and the axon terminals of 20 types of dopaminergic neurons (DANs).
source: In each MB, the parallel axonal fibers of ~2000 KCs can be divided into 16 compartmental units by the dendrites of 21 types of MB output neurons (MBONs) and the axon terminals of 20 types of dopaminergic neurons (DANs).
evidence: This claim is based on prior light microscopy studies of MB anatomy.

claim: Anatomical compartments in the MB are also parallel units of associative learning.
source: A large body of behavioral and physiological studies suggests that these anatomical compartments are also parallel units of associative learning (see e.g. Hige et al., 2015a; Lin et al., 2014b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral and physiological studies.

claim: DAN input to a compartment induces enduring changes in efficacy of KC>MBON synapses in those specific KCs that were active in that compartment at the time of dopamine release.
source: DAN input to a compartment has been shown to induce enduring changes in efficacy of KC>MBONs synapses in those specific KCs that were active in that compartment at the time of dopamine release (Hige et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior physiological studies.

claim: The valence of the memory is determined by which compartment receives dopamine during training, while the sensory specificity of the memory is determined by which KCs were active during training.
source: The valence of the memory appears to be determined by which compartment receives dopamine during training, while the sensory specificity of the memory is determined by which KCs were active during training (Liu et al., 2012; Heisenberg, 2003; Burke et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: The DANs which project to the α1 compartment play a key role in the formation of appetitive long-term memory of nutritional foods.
source: The DANs which project to the α1 compartment, the ventral-most compartment of the vertical lobe (Figure 1), play a key role in the formation of appetitive long-term memory of nutritional foods (Yamagata et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior behavioral studies.

claim: DANs that project to the α2 and α3 compartments play roles in aversive long-term memory.
source: DANs that project to the other α lobe compartments, α2 and α3, play roles in aversive long-term memory (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Séjourné et al., 2011; Pai et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: All three α lobe compartments receive feedforward inputs from GABAergic and glutamatergic MBONs whose dendrites lie in other MB compartments.
source: All three of these compartments receive feedforward inputs from GABAergic and glutamatergic MBONs whose dendrites lie in other MB compartments (Aso et al., 2014a) known to be involved in aversive or appetitive memory (Aso and Rubin, 2016; Aso et al., 2010; Burke et al., 2012; Perisse et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical and behavioral studies.

claim: MB-APL is a large GABAergic neuron that sends arbors throughout the MB-lobes and provides negative feedback important for sparse coding.
source: In addition, two types of MB-intrinsic neurons send arbors throughout the MB-lobes: a large GABAergic neuron, MB-APL, which provides negative feedback important for sparse coding (Papadopoulou et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2014a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior physiological studies.

claim: The MB-DPM neuron is involved in memory consolidation and sleep regulation.
source: and the MB-DPM neuron, which is involved in memory consolidation and sleep regulation (Waddell et al., 2000; Keene et al., 2006; Haynes et al., 2015; Yu et al., 2005a; Cervantes-Sandoval and Davis, 2012; Keene et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral and physiological studies.

claim: Previous EM studies in the MB lobes of various insects identified KCs by their abundance, fasciculating axons and small size.
source: Previous EM studies in the MB lobes of cockroaches (Mancini and Frontali, 1970, Mancini and Frontali, 1967), locusts (Leitch and Laurent, 1996), crickets, ants, honey bees (Schürmann, 1974, 2016) and Drosophila (Technau, 1984) identified KCs by their abundance, fasciculating axons and small size.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior EM studies.

claim: Leitch and Laurent (1996) identified large GABA immunoreactive neurons that contact KC axons in the locust pedunculus.
source: Additionally, Leitch and Laurent (1996) identified large GABA immunoreactive neurons that contact KC axons in the locust pedunculus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior EM study.

claim: A dense reconstruction of the three compartments that make up the α lobe of an adult Drosophila male was performed.
source: In this paper, we report a dense reconstruction of the three compartments that make up the α lobe of an adult Drosophila male (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is based on the methods and results described in the manuscript.

claim: The dense reconstruction provides confidence that all cell types with processes in the α lobe have been identified.
source: Because we performed a dense reconstruction, with the goal of determining the morphology and connectivity of all cells in the volume, we have confidence that we have identified all cell types with processes in the α lobe.
evidence: This claim is based on the completeness of the reconstruction effort.

claim: Cell-type-specific rescue of dopamine receptor mutants suggests that dopamine acts presynaptically in the KCs of KC>MBON synapses.
source: Cell-type-specific rescue of dopamine receptor mutants suggests that dopamine acts presynaptically in the KCs of KC>MBON synapses (Kim et al., 2007; Qin et al., 2012a; Liu et al., 2012; Ichinose et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior genetic studies.

claim: Postsynaptic mechanisms for dopamine action have also been proposed.
source: However, postsynaptic mechanisms have also been proposed (Cassenaer and Laurent, 2012; Pai et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A recent study detected expression of dopamine receptors in MBONs.
source: and a recent study detected expression of dopamine receptors in MBONs (Crocker et al., 2016), raising the possibility that MBONs might also be direct targets of DAN modulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior molecular study.

claim: Behavioral, imaging and electrophysiological data indicate that dopamine modulation respects the borders between compartments.
source: Behavioral, imaging and electrophysiological data (Aso et al., 2010; Hige et al., 2015a; Cohn et al., 2015) indicate that dopamine modulation respects the borders between compartments
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The brain of a 5-day-old adult male fly was imaged by focused ion-beam milling scanning electron microscopy (FIBSEM) over a 5-week imaging run.
source: The brain of a 5-day-old adult male fly was fixed, embedded and trimmed as described in Materials and methods. A ~40 × 50 x 120 μm volume (Figure 1B) encompassing the vertical lobe of the MB was imaged by focused ion-beam milling scanning electron microscopy (FIBSEM) (Xu et al., 2017) over a 5-week imaging run (Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is based on the methods described in the manuscript.

claim: The assembled volume has isotropic voxels (8 × 8 × 8 nm).
source: The assembled volume has isotropic voxels (8 × 8 × 8 nm) allowing image data to be viewed with the same resolution along any axis.
evidence: This claim is based on the imaging parameters used.

claim: A total of ~8 person years was devoted to proofreading the automated segmentation and synapse detection results.
source: The results of these automated processes were then reviewed and edited by trained human proofreaders; a total of ~8 person years was devoted to proofreading.
evidence: This claim is based on the effort invested in data curation.

claim: Only one cell type in the EM reconstructions had not been described at the light level: MBON-α2sp.
source: We found only one cell type in our EM reconstructions that had not been described at the light level, a single MBON that we named (MBON-α2sp).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of EM reconstructions with prior light microscopy data.

claim: 949 KCs were reconstructed in the α lobe.
source: We reconstructed 949 KCs in the α lobe, a number that agrees well with the previous estimate of ~1000 α/β KCs obtained by counting genetically labeled cell nuclei with light microscopy (Aso et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is based on direct counting in the EM reconstruction.

claim: 78 neurons were assigned to the α/βp KC class.
source: The α/βp cells are clearly distinct in both morphology and synaptic connectivity (see below) and we assigned 78 neurons to this class, compared to ~90 estimated by Aso et al. (2014a).
evidence: This claim is based on morphological and connectivity analysis in the EM reconstruction.

claim: The α3 compartment contains two PPL1-α3 DANs and two MBON-α3 cells.
source: The α3 compartment at the tip of the α lobe contains two PPL1-α3 DANs and two MBON-α3 cells (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This claim is based on cell identification in the EM reconstruction and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The α2 compartment has two PPL1-α′2α2 DANs and four MBONs of three distinct types.
source: The α2 compartment has two PPL1-α′2α2 DANs (neurons that innervate both the α2 compartment and the α′2 compartment of the α′ lobe) and four MBONs of three distinct types that differ based on the KCs they receive input from: one MBON-α2sc, two MBON-α2p3p and one MBON-α2sp (Figure 2I–L).
evidence: This claim is based on cell identification in the EM reconstruction and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The α1 compartment has 16 PAM-α1 DANs and 2 MBON-α1 cells.
source: The α1 compartment has 16 PAM-α1 DANs and 2 MBON-α1 cells (Figure 2M–O; Video 5).
evidence: This claim is based on cell identification in the EM reconstruction and shown in Figure 2.

claim: There are six additional cells with arbors in the α lobe that innervate all three compartments: ipsilateral APL, DPM, a SIFamide neuron, ipsilateral MBON-β1>α, and ipsi- and contralateral MBON-γ1pedc>α/β.
source: There are six additional cells with arbors in the α lobe, and each innervates all three compartments (Figure 2B–F): the ipsilateral APL and DPM, MB-intrinsic neurons that arborize widely throughout the MB lobes; a neuron expressing the neuropeptide SIFamide that arborizes broadly throughout the brain (Park et al., 2014; Verleyen et al., 2004); and the axons of the ipsilateral MBON-β1>α and the ipsi- and contralateral MBON-γ1pedc>α/β, which project from other MB lobes.
evidence: This claim is based on cell identification in the EM reconstruction and shown in Figure 2.

claim: In total, 983 neurons were reconstructed and identified in the α lobe.
source: In total, we reconstructed and identified portions of 983 neurons in the α lobe.
evidence: This claim is based on the complete count of identified neurons in the reconstruction.

claim: There are no other cell types with significant arborization in the α lobe beyond those identified.
source: Since we accounted for all major neurites and neuronal profiles and had only small fragmented bodies left unassigned to a specific neuronal type in the reconstructed volume (see below for the quantitative estimate), we are confident that there are no other cell types with significant arborization in the α lobe.
evidence: This claim is based on the completeness of the reconstruction and the small fraction of unassigned fragments.

claim: 89,406 presynaptic densities were identified in the α lobe.
source: We identified 89,406 presynaptic densities (Figures 4 and 5), using a combination of machine learning algorithms and human annotation.
evidence: This claim is based on synapse annotation in the EM reconstruction.

claim: 224,697 postsynaptic sites were manually annotated in the α lobe.
source: We then manually annotated a total of 224,697 postsynaptic sites in the α lobe, based primarily on their adjacency to a presynaptic density (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is based on synapse annotation in the EM reconstruction.

claim: 93% of postsynaptic sites could be traced back to the main arbors of an identified cell.
source: Of these postsynaptic sites, 93% could be traced back to the main arbors of an identified cell.
evidence: This claim is based on the tracing and assignment of postsynaptic sites.

claim: For 86% of synapses, the cell types of both the pre- and postsynaptic cells were identified.
source: For 86% of synapses, we were able to identify the cell types of both the pre- and postsynaptic cells.
evidence: This claim is based on the completeness of cell identification in the reconstruction.

claim: KCs frequently form rosette-like structures where multiple KCs make adjacent synapses onto an MBON dendritic process.
source: We frequently observed two or more KCs making adjacent synapses onto a dendritic process of an MBON, often making rosette-like structures that can also include DAN synapses (Figures 4A–C and and 5A,B; Video 6).
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of synaptic structures in the EM reconstruction.

claim: 80–93% of KC>MBON synapses are part of a convergence structure.
source: The highest percentage observed was for KC>MBON synapses, where 80–93% (depending on the MBON) of the 54,234 KC pre-synaptic sites that connect to MBONs are part of a convergence
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of synaptic structures in the EM reconstruction.

claim: 62% of KC>MBON synapses are part of a rosette structure.
source: and 62% part of a rosette.
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of synaptic structures in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Both clear and dense core synaptic vesicles (DCVs) were observed in early EM studies on the cockroach MB.
source: Both clear and dense core synaptic vesicles (DCVs) were observed in early EM studies on the cockroach MB (Mancini and Frontali, 1970, Mancini and Frontali, 1967).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior EM studies.

claim: The presynaptic sites of all reconstructed cell types except the SIFamide neuron contain at least two morphologically distinct classes of synaptic vesicles.
source: We found that the presynaptic sites of all reconstructed cell types except the SIFamide neuron contain at least two morphologically distinct classes of synaptic vesicles (Table 1; Figure 5E), suggesting that most cell types in the MB use multiple neurotransmitters.
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of vesicle morphology in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Most cell types in the MB use multiple neurotransmitters.
source: We found that the presynaptic sites of all reconstructed cell types except the SIFamide neuron contain at least two morphologically distinct classes of synaptic vesicles (Table 1; Figure 5E), suggesting that most cell types in the MB use multiple neurotransmitters.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of multiple vesicle types in most cell types.

claim: SIFamide neurons contain only large dense-core vesicles (roughly 125 nm in diameter).
source: SIFamide neurons contain only large dense-core vesicles (roughly 125 nm in diameter), while all other cells contain both DCVs and 45 nm diameter clear synaptic vesicles (Figure 5E; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of vesicle morphology in the EM reconstruction.

claim: All cells except SIFamide neurons contain both DCVs and 45 nm diameter clear synaptic vesicles.
source: SIFamide neurons contain only large dense-core vesicles (roughly 125 nm in diameter), while all other cells contain both DCVs and 45 nm diameter clear synaptic vesicles (Figure 5E; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of vesicle morphology in the EM reconstruction.

claim: The DCVs are 80 nm diameter in KCs, PPL1-α′2α2, PAM-α1, MBON-β1>α, APL, and DPM.
source: The DCVs are 80 nm diameter in KCs, PPL1-α′2α2, PAM- α1, MBON-β1>α, APL, and DPM, while those in PPL1-α3 are larger with a diameter of close to 100 nm (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on measurements of vesicle size in the EM reconstruction.

claim: DCVs in PPL1-α3 are larger with a diameter of close to 100 nm.
source: The DCVs are 80 nm diameter in KCs, PPL1-α′2α2, PAM- α1, MBON-β1>α, APL, and DPM, while those in PPL1-α3 are larger with a diameter of close to 100 nm (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on measurements of vesicle size in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Relatively few DCVs were found in APL, and almost none in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β.
source: We found relatively few DCVs in APL, and almost none in MBON-γ1pedc>α/β (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative observation of vesicle types in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Each of the three compartments has access to similar sensory information.
source: We found that each of the three compartments has access to similar sensory information.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of KC connectivity patterns across compartments.

claim: Every KC makes multiple en passant synapses in each compartment as KC axons pass through the compartments.
source: As KC axons pass through the compartments, every KC makes multiple en passant synapses in each compartment (Figure 5C,D; Table 2; Videos 8, 9 and 10).
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of KC synapses in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Every KC made synapses onto each of the MBONs in the α3 and α1 compartments.
source: Every KC made synapses onto each of these MBONs, averaging 28 ± 8 in the α3 compartment and 20 ± 6 in α1.
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of KC>MBON connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: The distribution of the number of synapses each KC makes with MBONs showed a close match to a Poisson distribution.
source: Interestingly, the data showed a close match to a Poisson distribution, as expected if each KC>MBON synapse is formed during development without regard to the placement of other KC synapses on the same MBON (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of synapse counts in the EM reconstruction.

claim: MBONs in α3 and α1 appear to integrate information from every KC and all KC classes that are found in their compartment.
source: Despite the fact we could find little statistical structure to describe the synaptic connectivity, KC>MBON convergence was, nevertheless, high enough that these MBONs appear to integrate information from every KC and all KC classes that are found in their compartment.
evidence: This claim is based on the completeness of KC>MBON connectivity observed in the EM reconstruction.

claim: MBON-α2p3p receives more than 75% of its input from α/βp KCs.
source: For example, MBON-α2p3p receives more than 75% of its input from α/βp KCs, which constitute only 8% of αlobe KCs.
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: α/βp KCs are not activated by odors.
source: Interestingly, the α/βp KCs are not activated by odors (Perisse et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior physiological study.

claim: MBON-α2sc receives inputs almost exclusively from α/βsc KCs whose dendrites lie in the main calyx and receive inputs primarily from olfactory projection neurons.
source: On the other hand, MBON-α2sc receives inputs almost exclusively from α/βsc KCs whose dendrites lie in the main calyx and receive inputs primarily from olfactory projection neurons.
evidence: This claim is based on connectivity analysis in the EM reconstruction combined with prior anatomical knowledge.

claim: MBON-α2p3p and MBON-α2sc have a strong bias in how they sample modalities of sensory information.
source: Thus, our reconstructions indicate that MBON-α2p3p and MBON-α2sc have a strong bias in how they sample modalities of sensory information.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the differential KC inputs to these MBONs.

claim: MBONs that project extensively to a particular sub-region connect to every KC within that subregion.
source: Despite this biased sampling, MBONs that project extensively to a particular sub-region connect to every KC within that subregion (Table 3).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: DANs make synaptic contacts with a variety of postsynaptic partners, including axo-axonal contacts with the presynaptic terminals of KCs.
source: Reconstructions of dopaminergic input to the α lobe showed that these cells make synaptic contacts with a variety of postsynaptic partners, including axo-axonal contacts with the presynaptic terminals of KCs.
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of DAN synapses in the EM reconstruction.

claim: DANs primarily target KCs, but also make many contacts with MBONs.
source: They primarily target KCs, but surprisingly also make many contacts with MBONs.
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of DAN connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: DAN>KC synapses are far fewer than KC>MBON synapses, numbering only about 10% by comparison.
source: While KCs are the main target of DANs, DAN>KC synapses are far fewer than KC>MBON synapses, numbering only about 10% by comparison (Tables 2 and 4).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative comparison of synapse counts in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Only 6% of KC>MBON synapses have a DAN terminal within a radius of 300 nm.
source: In fact, only 6% of KC>MBON synapses (3825 out of 61486) have a DAN terminal within a radius of 300 nm.
evidence: This claim is based on spatial analysis of synapse locations in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Electrophysiology data indicate that DANs induce strong synaptic depression at the KC>MBON synapse, suggesting that the great majority of synapses are affected.
source: Despite this, electrophysiology data indicate that DANs induce strong synaptic depression at the KC>MBON synapse, suggesting that the great majority of synapses are affected (Hige et al., 2015a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior physiological study.

claim: The dopaminergic modulation of KC>MBON synapses occurs by volume, rather than local, transmission of dopamine.
source: and, in turn, implying that the dopaminergic modulation of KC>MBON synapses occurs by volume, rather than local, transmission of dopamine.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the spatial distribution of DAN synapses relative to KC>MBON synapses.

claim: The nearest DAN>KC synapse can often be distant from a given KC>MBON synapse; on average, the closest DAN>KC synapse falls outside a radius of 800 nm from the given KC>MBON synapse.
source: Consistent with this view, the nearest DAN>KC synapse can often be distant from a given KC>MBON synapse; on average, the closest DAN>KC synapse falls outside a radius of 800 nm from the given KC>MBON synapse, with more than 10 other synapses (typically KC>KC, KC>MBON or KC>DAN) interspersed.
evidence: This claim is based on spatial analysis of synapse locations in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Not all KCs receive synaptic input from a DAN.
source: Moreover, while every KC makes multiple synapses onto the MBONs in each compartment (Table 3), not all KCs receive synaptic input from a DAN (Table 4).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of DAN>KC connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: In α2, 23.5% of the KCs lack synapses from a DAN.
source: For example, in α2, 23.5% of the KCs lack synapses from a DAN.
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of DAN>KC connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Both APL and DPM get many inputs from KCs.
source: Both cell types get many inputs from KCs, which would allow them to evaluate the overall activity in the MB.
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Both APL and DPM receive input from DANs in all three compartments.
source: They both also receive input from DANs in all three compartments (Table 5); however, these were far fewer than the number of synapses the DANs made onto the MBONs in each compartment (Table 6).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: APL sends no output to any DANs and no MBONs other than a few connections to MBON-α1.
source: In fact, APL sends no output to any DANs and no MBONs other than a few connections to MBON-α1 (Table 5).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of APL output connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: APL's role seems largely confined to influencing the sensory input the KCs convey to the lobes.
source: Thus, APL's role seems largely confined to influencing the sensory input the KCs convey to the lobes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the output connectivity pattern of APL.

claim: DPM makes synapses onto MBONs and DANs in all three α-lobe compartments.
source: On the other hand, DPM makes synapses onto MBONs and DANs in all three α-lobe compartments (Table 5).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of DPM output connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: The output profiles of APL and DPM were quite similar across all three compartments, except for the high number of connections between DPM and the two MBON-α1s.
source: Overall, the output profiles of these cells were quite similar across all three compartments. The only exception to this was the high number of connections we observed between DPM and the two MBON-α1s (Table 5)
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of connectivity patterns in the EM reconstruction.

claim: DPM has been shown to play a role in consolidation of long-term appetitive memory.
source: we note that DPM has been shown to play a role in consolidation of long-term appetitive memory (Krashes and Waddell, 2008), a process that takes place in the α1 compartment (Ichinose et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Both DPM and APL have modular anatomy.
source: One surprising finding from our reconstructions that was not visible from confocal imaging of these cells was that both DPM and APL have modular anatomy.
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of cell morphology in the EM reconstruction.

claim: The DPM arbor splits outside the MB lobe into three large branches which ramify within distinct zones of the α lobe.
source: The DPM arbor splits outside the MB lobe into three large branches which ramify within distinct zones of the α lobe; one branch innervates α1 and two others α2 and α3 (color-coded in Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of DPM morphology in the EM reconstruction.

claim: APL sends a series of separate processes that project through the α lobe, but these individual branches are not connected inside the α lobe.
source: In contrast, APL sends a series of separate processes that project through the α lobe, but these individual branches are not connected inside the α lobe (Video 11).
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of APL morphology in the EM reconstruction.

claim: KCs made direct synaptic connections to DANs.
source: Most strikingly, KCs made direct synaptic connections to DANs (Figure 4E; Table 7).
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of synaptic connections in the EM reconstruction.

claim: The number of KC>DAN synapses is larger than the number of DAN>KC synapses in all three compartments.
source: Indeed, the number of KC>DAN synapses is larger than the number of DAN>KC synapses (5037 vs. 2982 in α3; 1699 vs. 1466 in α2; and 3054 vs. 2011 in α1).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative comparison of synapse counts in the EM reconstruction.

claim: There are many direct DAN>MBON synaptic connections.
source: One of the more surprising findings here was our observation that there are many direct DAN>MBON synaptic connections.
evidence: This claim is based on direct observation of synaptic connections in the EM reconstruction.

claim: DAN>MBON connections are relatively strong excitatory inputs based on functional connectivity measures.
source: Moreover, our functional connectivity measures indicate that these were relatively strong excitatory inputs.
evidence: This claim is based on calcium imaging and electrophysiology experiments.

claim: The excitatory sign of the DAN>MBON connection is consistent with the behavioral effects of DAN activation.
source: The excitatory sign of the DAN>MBON connection is also consistent with the behavioral effects of DAN activation we observed (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is based on behavioral experiments showing effects of DAN activation on memory expression.

claim: A 100 msec photostimulation of PAM-α1 evoked a slow calcium rise in the MBON-α1.
source: A 100 msec photostimulation of PAM-α1 evoked a slow calcium rise in the MBON-α1 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is based on calcium imaging experiments.

claim: It took a few seconds for GCaMP fluorescence to reach peak amplitude after PAM-α1 stimulation, which then slowly decayed over ~20 s.
source: It took a few seconds for GCaMP fluorescence to reach peak amplitude, which then slowly decayed over ~20 s.
evidence: This claim is based on calcium imaging experiments.

claim: A two msec photo-stimulation of PAM-α1 evoked a slow depolarization in MBON-α1, of sufficient amplitude to elicit a spiking response.
source: With whole-cell recordings from MBON-α1, we observed that a two msec photo-stimulation of PAM-α1 also evoked a slow depolarization, of sufficient amplitude to elicit a spiking response.
evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiology experiments.

claim: DAN stimulation in the presence of tetrodotoxin and mecamylamine elicited a slow depolarizing response in MBON-α1, indicating monosynaptic excitatory transmission from DAN to MBON.
source: In contrast, DAN stimulation in the same conditions elicited a slow depolarizing response (Figure 7C,D), indicating that there is monosynaptic excitatory transmission from DAN to MBON.
evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiology experiments with pharmacological blockers.

claim: The MBON response to DAN stimulation was strongly diminished by the addition of a D1 dopamine receptor antagonist.
source: The response was strongly (although not completely) diminished by the addition of a D1 dopamine receptor antagonist (Figure 7E,F), indicating that DAN>MBON transmission acts largely through dopamine receptors (Boto et al., 2014; Sitaraman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is based on electrophysiology experiments with pharmacological antagonist.

claim: Activation of PAM-α1 during memory recall suppressed the conditioned approach response to the odor.
source: We found that activation suppressed the conditioned approach response to the odor (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This claim is based on behavioral experiments.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PPL1-α3 during memory recall suppressed expression of the induced aversive memory.
source: Similarly, when we examined the effects on memory recall with a 1-day-old memory from optogenetic training in the α3 compartment, we again found DAN activation suppressed expression of the induced aversive memory (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is based on behavioral experiments.

claim: Optogenetic activation of PPL1-α3 alone or in combination with other PPL1 DANs, in the absence of odor presentation, produced an attraction response.
source: We also found that optogenetic activation of PPL1-α3 alone or in combination with other PPL1 DANs, in the absence of odor presentation, produced an attraction response (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is based on behavioral experiments.

claim: The primary synaptic targets of feedforward neurons MBON-β1>α and MBON-γ1pedc>α/β are the MBONs in the downstream compartment.
source: Our connectome results show that the primary synaptic targets of these feedforward neurons are the MBONs in the downstream compartment (Table 5).
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: Relatively few connections from feedforward MBONs onto KCs were observed.
source: By contrast, we observed relatively few connections onto KCs.
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: The feedforward connections can strongly influence the output from a compartment, but likely have little impact on the sensory information delivered to each compartment from the KCs.
source: Overall, this suggests that the feedforward connections can strongly influence the output from a compartment, but likely have little impact on the sensory information delivered to each compartment from the KCs.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the connectivity patterns of feedforward MBONs.

claim: In α1, the terminals of MBON-β1>α are concentrated on a region of the MBON-α1 dendrites closest to the cell's axon.
source: In α1, the terminals of MBON-β1>α are concentrated on a region of the MBON-α1 dendrites closest to the cell's axon, a cellular location that might provide a strong influence on the cell's spiking output (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is based on spatial analysis of synapse locations in the EM reconstruction.

claim: MBON-β1>α is nearly four times more likely to make synapses onto MBON-γ1pedc>α/β than vice versa in the α2 and α3 compartments.
source: The MBON-β1>α and MBON-γ1pedc>α/β feedforward neurons also make synapses onto each other, but in an asymmetric manner: MBON-β1>α is nearly four times more likely to make synapses onto MBON-γ1pedc>α/β than vice versa in the α2 and α3 compartments (Figures 4F and 9D; Table 5
evidence: This claim is based on quantitative analysis of connectivity in the EM reconstruction.

claim: The basic wiring motifs were very similar in each compartment.
source: There is no simple explanation for these differences from the EM-level circuit structure, as the basic wiring motifs were very similar in each compartment.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of connectivity patterns across compartments in the EM reconstruction.

claim: The size of dense core vesicles differs between DANs innervating the different compartments.
source: The size of these vesicles differs between DANs innervating the different compartments (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is based on measurements of vesicle size in the EM reconstruction.

claim: If the synaptic depression observed at KC>MBON synapses also acts at KC>DAN connections, odor-evoked DAN responses would be diminished as a result of learning.
source: If the synaptic depression observed at KC>MBON synapses also acts at KC>DAN connections, odor-evoked DAN responses would be diminished as a result of learning.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the observed KC>DAN connections and known plasticity at KC>MBON synapses.

claim: A gradually plateauing of the learning curve is a common feature of memory formation in different systems, including olfactory conditioning in Drosophila.
source: Indeed, a gradually plateauing of the learning curve is a common feature of memory formation in different systems (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972; Bush and Mosteller, 1951), including olfactory conditioning in Drosophila (Tully and Quinn, 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: The slow synaptic dynamics observed in the DAN>MBON connection suggest the possibility that small changes in DAN firing might be capable of producing sustained changes in MBON membrane potential reflecting the current internal state of the animal.
source: The slow synaptic dynamics we observed in the DAN>MBON connection in MBON-α1 (Figure 7) suggest the possibility that small changes in DAN firing might be capable of producing sustained changes in MBON membrane potential reflecting the current internal state of the animal.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the observed slow dynamics of DAN>MBON transmission.

claim: Prior work on odor-sugar conditioning in larvae provided evidence that flies form a comparison between the current state of reward and the reward expected from the conditioned cue.
source: In Drosophila, prior work on odor-sugar conditioning in larvae provided evidence that flies form a comparison between the current state of reward and the reward expected from the conditioned cue (Schleyer et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a prior behavioral study.

claim: Animals behaviorally express memories only when the expected reward intensity is higher than the currently available reward.
source: This work showed that animals behaviorally express memories only when the expected reward intensity is higher than the currently available reward (Schleyer et al., 2011, Schleyer et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: Most sparse tracing strategies would have discovered the new pathways reported in this study.
source: It is likely that most sparse tracing strategies would have discovered the new pathways reported here, as the connections are numerous and connect well known cell types.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about alternative approaches to connectomics.

claim: A rare cell type, such as the SIFamide neuron, might have been missed with sparse tracing.
source: Conversely, the conclusions that all cell types in this circuit had been identified would have been more difficult to make with confidence and a rare cell type, such as the SIFamide neuron, might have been missed.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the limitations of sparse tracing approaches.

claim: Statistical arguments that require an accurate assessment of which cells are not connected would have been hard to make from sparse tracing.
source: Perhaps, most importantly, statistical arguments, particularly those that require an accurate assessment of which cells are not connected, such as the absence of network structures such as rings or chains, would have been hard to make from sparse tracing.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the limitations of sparse tracing approaches.

claim: The model independent nature of dense tracing helps to discover any 'unknown unknowns', provides the strongest constraints on how neural circuits are constructed, and allows retrospective analysis of network properties not targeted during reconstruction.
source: More generally, the model independent nature of dense tracing helps to discover any 'unknown unknowns', provides the strongest constraints on how neural circuits are constructed, and allows retrospective analysis of network properties not targeted during reconstruction.
evidence: This claim is a general statement about the value of dense reconstruction approaches.

claim: The same novel connections found in the adult α lobe were also found in a parallel study of the larval MB.
source: We note that these same novel connections were also found in a parallel study of the larval MB (Eichler et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a parallel study.

claim: The relative prevalence of novel connections was strikingly similar between the larval MB and adult α lobe.
source: Not only were the same circuit motifs found in the larval MB and adult α lobe, but also the relative prevalence of these connections was strikingly similar: DAN>MBON synapses were 4.5% the number of KC>MBON synapses in the adult α lobe and 3.4% in the larval MB. KC>DAN synapses were 1.5 times as prevalent as DAN>KC synapses in the adult α lobe, as compared with 1.1 in the larval MB. KCs make 48% of their synapses onto other KCs in the adult α lobe and 45% in the larval upper vertical lobe compartments.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of quantitative connectivity data between the adult and larval MB.

claim: The conservation of the relative abundances of connections across developmental stages may reflect important functional constraints on the circuit.
source: It is tempting to speculate that the conservation of the relative abundances of these connections across developmental stages reflects important functional constraints on the circuit.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the observed conservation of connectivity patterns.

claim: 80–93% of KC>MBON synapses are part of a convergence, depending on the MBON.
source: The highest percentage observed was for KC>MBON synapses, where 80–93% (depending on the MBON) of the 54,234 KC pre-synaptic sites that connect to MBONs are part of a convergence
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of synaptic structures in the EM data.

claim: 60% of KC>DAN synapses are part of a convergence.
source: Other KC targets had a lower fraction of their synapses to KCs in rosettes: KC>DAN (60% convergence, 37% rosettes of 9615 pre-synaptic sites)
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of synaptic structures in the EM data.

claim: 37% of KC>DAN synapses are part of a rosette.
source: Other KC targets had a lower fraction of their synapses to KCs in rosettes: KC>DAN (60% convergence, 37% rosettes of 9615 pre-synaptic sites)
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of synaptic structures in the EM data.

claim: 69% of KC>APL synapses are part of a convergence.
source: APL (69% convergence, 32% rosettes of 9063 pre-synaptic sites)
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of synaptic structures in the EM data.

claim: 32% of KC>APL synapses are part of a rosette.
source: APL (69% convergence, 32% rosettes of 9063 pre-synaptic sites)
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of synaptic structures in the EM data.

claim: 56% of KC>DPM synapses are part of a convergence.
source: For DPM, in contrast, although 56% of its 7168 KC>DPM synapses were part of a convergence, only 12% were part of a rosette.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of synaptic structures in the EM data.

claim: 12% of KC>DPM synapses are part of a rosette.
source: For DPM, in contrast, although 56% of its 7168 KC>DPM synapses were part of a convergence, only 12% were part of a rosette.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of synaptic structures in the EM data.

claim: 55% of KC>KC synapses occur in rosettes.
source: Of KC>KC synapses, 55% occur in rosettes.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of synaptic structures in the EM data.

claim: Two KCs that participated in a rosette do not have an increased chance of converging again in a second rosette elsewhere in the α lobe.
source: We asked whether two KCs that participated in a rosette had an increased chance of converging again in a second rosette elsewhere in the αlobe; we found no such correlation.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of rosette participation patterns in the EM data.
